title: Cumulative resources: crews and outage windows

blocks.text: 4.5.2 Cumulative Resources: Crews and Outage Windows

Lesson 4.5.1 gave each crew its own calendar. GridCap's vegetation manager does not think that way: she has a **pool** of three crews for the season and twelve jobs, and some jobs need two crews at once. A corridor widening (P006, P012, P020, P035) runs a mower and a climbing crew side by side, so it takes two of the three crews for its whole length; a circuit job takes one. Her questions are about the pool: "in any week, do the jobs under way need more crews than I have?", "what if one crew is held back for storm duty in the stormy weeks?", "can my circuit clears fit into the weeks the grid operators will switch those circuits off?". (GridCap is fictional; so is this season, see `season.py` in lesson 4.5.1.)
Each question is a resource with a capacity, and CP-SAT states each in one constraint. The twelve jobs come from `season.py`:

P003 Valley circuit  clear weeks 2  crews 1  due 20  weight 10
P004 Plains circuit  trim  weeks 6  crews 1  due  6  weight 30
P006 Valley corridor widen weeks 4  crews 2  due  6  weight  6
P008 Ridge  circuit  clear weeks 6  crews 1  due  6  weight 13
P010 Valley circuit  clear weeks 4  crews 1  due 12  weight 28
P011 Coast  circuit  trim  weeks 4  crews 1  due  6  weight 11
P012 Coast  corridor widen weeks 6  crews 2  due  6  weight 22
P014 Coast  circuit  trim  weeks 2  crews 1  due 20  weight 38
P015 Coast  circuit  clear weeks 2  crews 1  due 12  weight 31
P018 Valley circuit  clear weeks 6  crews 1  due 20  weight 30
P020 Ridge  corridor widen weeks 2  crews 2  due 20  weight 15
P035 Ridge  corridor widen weeks 6  crews 2  due 20  weight 13

`crews` is the job's **demand**: how many of the pool's crews it holds in every week it runs. The due weeks and weights are for lesson 4.5.4; this lesson minimizes the makespan, the week the last job ends, as lesson 4.5.1 did.
Cumulative Caps the Crews at Work in Every Week

`NoOverlap` says "at most one at a time". The pool needs "at most three crews' worth at a time", where each job counts its demand. That is the **cumulative** constraint. Given intervals $`[s_j, s_j + d_j)`$, demands $`c_j`$ and a capacity $`K`$, it requires that in every week $`w`$ the demands of the jobs running in that week add up to at most $`K`$:
\sum_{j \in J \,:\, s_j \le w < s_j + d_j} c_j \;\le\; K \qquad \forall w

The set under the sum depends on the starts, which are variables, so this is not a linear row you could hand to a MIP solver as written. CP-SAT takes it as one constraint, `add_cumulative(intervals, demands, capacity)`, and reasons about it directly. `season_model.build` creates one fixed-size interval per job on a start variable and adds the pool:

s.start[j.jid] = model.new_int_var(0, horizon - j.weeks, f"start_{j.jid}")
s.task[j.jid] = model.new_fixed_size_interval_var(s.start[j.jid], j.weeks, f"work_{j.jid}")
intervals = [s.task[j.jid] for j in jobs]
demands = [j.crews for j in jobs]
model.add_cumulative(intervals, demands, crews)
The start's upper bound is `horizon - j.weeks`, so every job ends inside the 30-week season. The makespan objective is the one of lesson 4.5.1, written with the interval's end expression:

def minimize_makespan(s: Season, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> None:
    s.makespan = s.model.new_int_var(0, horizon, "makespan")
    s.model.add_max_equality(s.makespan, [s.end(j.jid) for j in s.jobs])
    s.model.minimize(s.makespan)

`crew_pool.py` first works out a bound by hand. The twelve jobs need 68 crew-weeks (weeks times demand, summed), and three crews supply 3 crew-weeks per week, so no schedule can end before week $`\lceil 68 / 3 \rceil = 23`$:

12 jobs, 68 crew-weeks of work, 3 crews: no schedule ends before week 23
OPTIMAL: makespan 24 weeks
  P004 Plains trim  crews 1  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P012 Coast  widen crews 2  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P008 Ridge  clear crews 1  weeks  6-11  due  6  late 6 x 13
  P035 Ridge  widen crews 2  weeks  6-11  due 20
  P010 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 12-15  due 12  late 4 x 28
  P011 Coast  trim  crews 1  weeks 12-15  due  6  late 10 x 11
  P018 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 12-17  due 20
  P006 Valley widen crews 2  weeks 16-19  due  6  late 14 x 6
  P003 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 18-19  due 20
  P014 Coast  trim  crews 1  weeks 20-21  due 20  late 2 x 38
  P015 Coast  clear crews 1  weeks 20-21  due 12  late 10 x 31
  P020 Ridge  widen crews 2  weeks 22-23  due 20  late 4 x 15
crews at work by week: 333333333333333333332222000000

The last line is the **load profile**: the crews at work in each of the 30 weeks, one digit per week. It never exceeds 3, which is the cumulative constraint at work, and it is full for the first 20 weeks. The optimum is 24, one week above the hand bound, and `OPTIMAL` means CP-SAT proved that 23 is impossible. The hand bound only counts crew-weeks; it knows nothing about which jobs can share a week, so a real schedule can need more.
The `late` notes show what the makespan does not care about: P006 is due at week 6 and finishes at week 20. Lesson 4.5.4 changes the objective.
NoOverlap Is Cumulative With Capacity 1

A single crew is a pool of size 1 in which every job has demand 1, so `add_cumulative(intervals, [1] * n, 1)` must say exactly what `add_no_overlap(intervals)` says. `nooverlap_is_cumulative.py` solves the one-crew schedule of lesson 4.5.1 (five jobs, the training week and the storm standby) both ways:

add_no_overlap:                 makespan 18
add_cumulative, capacity 1:     makespan 18

The same 18 weeks. Use `add_no_overlap` when the capacity really is 1: it says what you mean, and CP-SAT has reasoning made for that case. Use `add_cumulative` when a resource holds more than one job, or when jobs take different amounts of it.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Capacity That Drops Is a Fixed Interval Holding the Missing Crews

From week 12 to week 15 the regional operations center holds one crew back for storm duty, so the pool has 2 crews in those 4 weeks and 3 the rest of the season. `add_cumulative` takes one capacity. How do you make it change over time?
Add a fixed interval for the period, with the demand of the crews that are away. It occupies part of the capacity just as a job would, and the jobs share what is left:

for first, (weeks, away) in (standby or {}).items():
    intervals.append(model.new_fixed_size_interval_var(first, weeks, f"standby_{first}"))
    demands.append(away)
model.add_cumulative(intervals, demands, crews)

Here `standby = {12: (4, 1)}` (`STANDBY` in `season_model.py`): from week 12, for 4 weeks, 1 crew away. The capacity stays at 3 (the most crews the season ever has), and a fixed interval of demand $`3 - a_w`$ is added wherever only $`a_w`$ crews are available. The OR-Tools sample `cumulative_variable_profile_sample_sat.py` builds a whole day's capacity profile this way, with one fixed interval per period, each as high as the gap between that period's capacity and the peak.

OPTIMAL: makespan 24 weeks
  P008 Ridge  clear crews 1  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P012 Coast  widen crews 2  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P018 Valley clear crews 1  weeks  6-11  due 20
  P035 Ridge  widen crews 2  weeks  6-11  due 20
  P004 Plains trim  crews 1  weeks 12-17  due  6  late 12 x 30
  P011 Coast  trim  crews 1  weeks 12-15  due  6  late 10 x 11
  P006 Valley widen crews 2  weeks 16-19  due  6  late 14 x 6
  P010 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 18-21  due 12  late 10 x 28
  P020 Ridge  widen crews 2  weeks 20-21  due 20  late 2 x 15
  P003 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 22-23  due 20  late 4 x 10
  P014 Coast  trim  crews 1  weeks 22-23  due 20  late 4 x 38
  P015 Coast  clear crews 1  weeks 22-23  due 12  late 12 x 31
crews at work by week: 333333333333222233333333000000
crews available:       333333333333222233333333333333

Weeks 12 to 15 now have 2 crews at work, and the profile never goes above the second line. The makespan is still 24. Count the crew-weeks: 24 weeks of 3 crews are 72, the work takes 68 and the standby 4, so this schedule leaves no crew idle before week 24, where the first one had 4 idle crew-weeks (weeks 20 to 23 at 2 crews). The schedule is a different one, and its late jobs differ: a rule that does not move the objective can still move the plan.
A capacity that *rises* over time works the same way: set the capacity to the highest level and hold the difference with fixed intervals in the weeks before it rises.
<!-- practice 2 -->
An Outage Window Is a Domain on the Start

A circuit **clear** (P003, P008, P010, P015, P018) removes trees close to energized conductors, so the circuit must be switched off (an **outage**) while the crew works. The grid operators allow outages only in certain weeks of each region, `OUTAGE_WINDOWS` in `season.py`: the Valley, for example, can be switched in weeks $`[2, 12)`$ and $`[18, 28)`$. A clear must lie entirely inside one window.

For a job of $`d`$ weeks and a window $`[a, b)`$, the starts that keep the job inside are $`a, a+1, \dots, b - d`$. The job's allowed starts are the union of those ranges over its region's windows: a set of integers with holes. CP-SAT lets a variable take its values from exactly such a set, a **domain**, built with `cp_model.Domain.from_intervals` and used through `new_int_var_from_domain`:

if outages and j.needs_outage:
    s.start[j.jid] = model.new_int_var_from_domain(start_domain(j, horizon), f"start_{j.jid}")

`Domain.from_intervals` takes closed ranges, both ends included, so $`[a, b - d]`$ here is the list `[a, b - j.weeks]`. A window shorter than the job is skipped (`b - j.weeks >= a`). The five clears get these domains:

P003 Valley 2 weeks  windows ((2, 12), (18, 28))  start in [2,10][18,26]
P008 Ridge  6 weeks  windows ((0, 8), (14, 24))  start in [0,2][14,18]
P010 Valley 4 weeks  windows ((2, 12), (18, 28))  start in [2,8][18,24]
P015 Coast  2 weeks  windows ((0, 10), (16, 30))  start in [0,8][16,28]
P018 Valley 6 weeks  windows ((2, 12), (18, 28))  start in [2,6][18,22]

P008 may start in weeks 0 to 2 or 14 to 18: a six-week clear starting at week 2 occupies $`[2, 8)`$, weeks 2 to 7, and its end, 8, equals the end of the first Ridge window $`[0, 8)`$, whose last week is 7. One starting at week 3 would also work week 8, which lies outside the window, when the circuit is back on.

No constraint was added: the windows live in the variable's domain, and a start in a hole is not a value the solver can even try. The OR-Tools sample `scheduling_with_calendar_sample_sat.py` does the same for a task that cannot start during a lunch break, with `Domain.from_intervals([(8, 12), (14, 15)])`.
One Outage per Region Is a NoOverlap Over That Region's Clears

The operators add one more rule: a region switches off one circuit at a time, so two clears in the same region must not overlap. That is a second resource, of capacity 1, over a subset of the same intervals:

An interval can sit in as many scheduling constraints as you like: each clear is in the crew pool's cumulative *and* in its region's NoOverlap, and the schedule must satisfy both. (A region with one clear needs no NoOverlap, hence `len(clears) > 1`.) `outages.py` solves the season with the standby and the windows, first without and then with the one-outage rule, and prints the clears:

windows only: OPTIMAL, makespan 24 weeks
  P008 Ridge  clear crews 1  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P010 Valley clear crews 1  weeks  2- 5  due 12
  P018 Valley clear crews 1  weeks  2- 7  due 20
  P015 Coast  clear crews 1  weeks  6- 7  due 12
  P003 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 22-23  due 20  late 4 x 10
windows, one outage per region: OPTIMAL, makespan 24 weeks
  P008 Ridge  clear crews 1  weeks  0- 5  due  6
  P018 Valley clear crews 1  weeks  4- 9  due 20
  P003 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 10-11  due 20
  P015 Coast  clear crews 1  weeks 16-17  due 12  late 6 x 31
  P010 Valley clear crews 1  weeks 18-21  due 12  late 10 x 28

Every clear sits inside a window of its region in both runs. With windows only, P010 and P018 both switch Valley circuits off in weeks 2 to 5; with the rule, the Valley's three clears run one after another. They need 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 weeks and the first Valley window is 10 weeks long, so one of them has to wait for the second window, $`[18, 28)`$: P010 does. The makespan is 24 in all four runs of this lesson. The rules cost no time at the end of the season, but they move jobs, and a moved job can be a late one; lesson 4.5.4 prices that.

Why a domain for the windows and not optional intervals, one per window with exactly one present, as lesson 4.5.1 chose crews? Both are correct. The domain is smaller (one variable, no Booleans). Optional intervals are worth their size when the choice of window must appear in other rules or in the objective: a different crew rate in the late window, for example.
<!-- practice 3 -->
The Model
The season model `season_model.build` writes with every option on, and the makespan objective of this lesson. This lesson added the pool, the standby and the outage rules.

**Sets.** $`J`$ the jobs; $`O \subseteq J`$ the circuit clears, which need an outage; $`R`$ the regions, with $`r(j)`$ the region of job $`j`$; $`\mathcal{W}_r`$ the outage windows of region $`r`$, each a span $`[a, b)`$ of weeks.

**Parameters.** $`d_j`$, the weeks of job $`j`$; $`c_j`$, the crews it holds while it runs; $`K = 3`$, the crews in the pool; $`H = 30`$, the season's weeks; the standby, $`n = 1`$ crew away for the 4 weeks $`[12, 16)`$.
**Variables.**
**Objective.**
\min \; C
**Constraints.** Each job's interval is $`[s_j, s_j + d_j)`$, a fixed-size interval on $`s_j`$.
$`[12 \le w < 16]`$ is 1 in the standby weeks and 0 otherwise: the standby's fixed interval.

rows: `add_cumulative(intervals, demands, crews)`, with the standby interval appended
`add_no_overlap(clears)`, for each region with two or more clears

blocks.text: Summary

items: **Cumulative caps the crews at work in every week.** `add_cumulative(intervals, demands, capacity)`: in every unit of time, the demands of the running intervals add up to at most the capacity.
**NoOverlap is cumulative with capacity 1** and every demand 1; use NoOverlap when that is what you mean.
**A capacity that drops is a fixed interval holding the missing crews.** Set the capacity to the peak and add a fixed interval with demand peak − available in each period below it.
**An outage window is a domain on the start.** `Domain.from_intervals` with closed ranges $`[a, b - d]`$, one per window, and `new_int_var_from_domain`.
**One outage per region is a NoOverlap over that region's clears.** One interval can belong to several resource constraints, and the schedule meets them all.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: sum of the demands of the intervals running at any time ≤ capacity
the integers in $`[a_1, b_1] \cup [a_2, b_2]`$, ends included
an integer variable whose values are the domain
the interval's end, as an expression
one crew, machine or circuit at a time
a pool of $`K`$ identical units, jobs taking $`c_j`$ each

blocks.text: **Further reading:** the CP-SAT samples [`cumulative_variable_profile_sample_sat.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/sat/samples/cumulative_variable_profile_sample_sat.py) (a capacity profile held by fixed intervals) and [`scheduling_with_calendar_sample_sat.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/sat/samples/scheduling_with_calendar_sample_sat.py) (a start domain with a hole); OR-Tools, [The Job Shop Problem](https://developers.google.com/optimization/scheduling/job_shop), for the NoOverlap-per-resource pattern this lesson extends; the CP-SAT Primer, [Advanced Modeling](https://d-krupke.github.io/cpsat-primer/advanced_modelling.html), on `add_cumulative` (demands and capacity may also be variables) and [Basic Modeling](https://d-krupke.github.io/cpsat-primer/modelling.html), on custom domains and their costs.
Challenges

items: Raise the pool to four crews in `crew_pool.py`. Work out the hand bound first, then run it.
Make the standby two crews instead of one. Predict whether the makespan moves, and check the load profile.
Give the Coast a single outage window, $`[0, 10)`$. Which clear can no longer be placed late, and what does the solver report if the Coast's clears cannot all fit?

blocks.text: Design Note: Domains Are Data, So Check Them as Data

An outage window that is one week too short, or a domain built with $`b`$ where $`b - d`$ was meant, does not make the model fail loudly. It makes some starts impossible, and the solver answers with a worse schedule or, if no start is left, `INFEASIBLE` with no hint of why. Print each domain next to its windows, as `outages.py` does, and test `start_domain` on a job whose length equals its window (exactly one start) and on one longer than every window (an empty domain). Lesson 4.6.2 shows how CP-SAT can name the rule that made a model infeasible.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**crew_pool.py.** The twelve jobs on a pool of three crews with one cumulative constraint, the hand bound, and the load profile (*Cumulative Caps the Crews at Work in Every Week*). *Try:* Make every corridor need 3 crews. Predict whether any two corridors can then run in the same week.

**nooverlap_is_cumulative.py.** The one-crew schedule of lesson 4.5.1 with NoOverlap and with a capacity-1 cumulative (*NoOverlap Is Cumulative With Capacity 1*). *Try:* Give the training week a demand of 1 and the capacity 2 in the cumulative version. Predict the makespan.

**crew_standby.py.** The pool with one crew held back in weeks 12 to 15 (*A Capacity That Drops Is a Fixed Interval Holding the Missing Crews*). *Try:* Move the standby to weeks 0 to 3. Predict whether the first two jobs change.

**outages.py.** The clears' start domains, then the season with outage windows, without and with one outage per region (*An Outage Window Is a Domain on the Start*, *One Outage per Region Is a NoOverlap Over That Region's Clears*). *Try:* Shorten the Valley's first window to $`[2, 8)`$. Predict which Valley clears can still go in it.
**season_model.py.** The model builder this lesson and lesson 4.5.4 use: one interval per job, the pool, the standby, the outage rules, and the two objectives. It runs nothing itself.
